question:
A 62-year-old male presents with a 4-month history of progressively worsening fatigue and decreased
appetite. He underwent a kidney transplant from a living relative five years ago and is currently on
sirolimus and mycophenolate therapy. His blood pressure is 134/89 mm Hg. Laboratory findings reveal
normocytic, normochromic anemia and a serum creatinine level of 3.1 mg/dL, whereas his vital signs
and lab results were normal six months ago. What is the most likely mechanism responsible for the
increase in this patient’s creatinine concentration? Answer Choices: (A) CD8+ T cell-mediated
parenchymal cell damage (B) Drug-induced tubular vacuolization (C) CD4+ T cell-mediated intimal
smooth muscle proliferation (D) Mycophenolate-associated bone marrow suppression leading to renal
hypoperfusion (E) Fibrosis secondary to recurrent glomerulonephritis (F) Chronic ischemic injury due to
donor-specific antibodies (G) Calcineurin inhibitor-induced vasoconstriction (H) Antibody-mediated
endothelial cell injury (I) Sirolimus-induced tubular epithelial cell apoptosis (J) Tubulointerstitial
inflammation from viral reactivation
 A. Antibody-mediated endothelial cell injury

B. Tubulointerstitial inflammation from viral reactivation
C. CD8+ T cell-mediated parenchymal cell damage
D. Drug-induced tubular vacuolization
E. Chronic ischemic injury due to donor-specific antibodies
F. Sirolimus-induced tubular epithelial cell apoptosis
G. Mycophenolate-associated bone marrow suppression leading to renal hypoperfusion
H. CD4+ T cell-mediated intimal smooth muscle proliferation
I. Calcineurin inhibitor-induced vasoconstriction
J. Fibrosis secondary to recurrent glomerulonephritis
